extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / scientists (members/readers of the Philosophical Transactions): astronomers, physiologists, experimentalists, engineers, and learned correspondents
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing or producing 17th-century natural philosophy reports (observational astronomy, experimental physiology, engineering descriptions) focusing on methods, measurements, and evidential reasoning. Emphasises how to record observations, describe apparatus/procedures, and marshal empirical indications in support of hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for computing tides at a locality
rubrics_metrics.description: By this method then may the time and height of the tides be with sufficient certainty computed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure mean, high, and low water depths on a perpendicular to the base (AB and CD in the figure). Use the moon's position (equinoctial points, tropical moons) to set circle radii and draw lines parallel to the base to intersect the perpendicular at predicted high/low water heights. Example numeric heights for the locality (mean ~15 ft, high ~24 ft, low ~6 ft) and worked construction are provided; author notes agreement with collected observations (e.g. Captain Knox) as validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites for digestion (anatomical/physiological necessities)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are likewise required these further requisites, in some, or in most creatures, 1. That the stomach receive a gentle heat from the liver. 2. That it have a natural situation. 3. That it be assisted by the omentum. 4. That the stomach have a tunica villosa. 5. Windings of the intestines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each listed requisite is offered as necessary to parallel the action of an artificial menstruum: tunica villosa facilitates parceling of meat, omentum and natural placement assist concoction, heat from liver supplies a gentle heat; windings slow passage to avoid perpetual hunger. The argument is drawn from comparative anatomy/behaviour (e.g. hares doubling hind legs) and functional analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of the natural stomachal ferment (gastric juice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients of the natural ferment I take to be these. The saliva, the succus of the glands of the stomach, and a nitro-aerial spirit of the nerves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author gives reasons: saliva aids mixing and is impregnated with a volatile salt (phosphate of ammonia); glands of the stomach likely secrete a fermenting liquor (correlated with voracity in species having many glands); nitro-aerial spirits invoked from Mayow's arguments, with cited chemical effects (corroding iron, dissolving compages) supporting a universal menstruum-like action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental procedure for producing artificial chyle (artificial digestion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The digesting liquor is prepared from spirit of sulphur, spirit of hartshorn, the chyle of a dog, and the saliva; into a dram of this liquor put a piece of veal about the size of a nut and set it on a digesting furnace; in two hours there came from the meat a liquor having the colour and taste of chyle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author records organoleptic and physical properties: menstruum pellucid, without smell, salt yields cubical crystals, taste like vomited meat, does not ferment with an alkali. Observations on different meats yield similar phenomena. Contrasts with trials using acids alone (which did not produce same phenomena) and notes limitations (doesn't assert liquid alone digests; other anatomical requisites needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidential criteria for gland function in stomach (anatomical observation standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of a large bed of glands near the pylorus: occupying about 1/4 of the inside of the stomach, brownish-red, divided into ridges parallel to the stomach, more moist where glands are, many blood-vessels behind the glands; portions of prey within gland region dissolved or turning into mucilage while more distal parts remain intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gross anatomical description (location, colour, ridging, relation to pylorus), vascularization, local moisture, and differential effect on included food as converging evidence that glands secrete a powerful menstruum involved in digestion. Dissections of stomachs filled with prey are used as functional demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary criteria for or against an acid gastric ferment
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments mixing stomach mucous (from jack or hedge-hog) with reagents (sublimate, syrup of violets) produced whitening or green colour changes; these are urged as an argument against the existence of an acid ferment in the stomach, suggesting a volatile alkali instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple qualitative chemical tests and colour changes to infer the chemical nature of gastric juice, but note cautions: difficulty obtaining pure gastric juice means the observed alkali may derive from dissolved alimentary substances; author notes the latter conjecture is most probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria/evidence for porosity of animal bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts of animals, especially whilst living, are furnished with numerous pores; this is deduced from the frame/constitution of stable parts, nature of nutrition, abundance of matter carried off by sweat and insensible transpiration, entrance of effluvia into animals (evident from operation of plasters and ointments), effects of pericarpia and cantharides, and excretion of matter by apices or urine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple converging physiological and practical phenomena (transpiration, absorption of effluvia, topical applications) and specific observations (mercury found in bones after ingestion) to argue for porosity. The approach is to marshal diverse lines of empirical evidence rather than a single experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria/evidence for porosity of solid bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Porosity of solid bodies is argued a priori (from origin/formation, disparities in specific gravities, constitution of particles not touching exactly) and a posteriori (experiments/observations on wood, earthen vessels, stones, metals, and glass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine theoretical reasoning about particulate structure with experimental demonstrations showing porous behaviour in materials assumed non-porous; both forms of argument are presented as valid evidence for porosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reporting eclipse observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Record precise corrected times for eclipse phases (beginning, centre immersion, greatest obscuration, centre emergence, end), quantify obscuration in 'digits' of the solar diameter, and compare observations from different sites with parallax reductions to deduce meridian differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples give times to the second, numbers of digits eclipsed, and tabulated observations from multiple locations; M. Cassini compares observations and performs parallax reductions to conclude differences of meridians. Emphasises precision in timing, standardised units (digits), and inter-site comparison with necessary geometric corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for measuring obliquity and ancient/modern observational practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use careful instruments (ring and table, long alhidade or paralactic ruler, large quadrants with arcs divided to seconds) and account for parallax and instrument precision when reporting obliquity of the ecliptic; later ages with better instruments correct ancient errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples cite Eratosthenes, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, and numerous oriental astronomers; authors note that some shorter tables omit seconds for brevity but precise measurements require division to seconds and consideration of horizontal parallax (example: Ebn Shatir's correction). The implicit standard is to use the largest practicable instruments and careful reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards/methods for describing and inferring the origin of a mineral (salt) spring
rubrics_metrics.description: Report location relative to town/river, seasonal visibility (visible only in summer when river discharge shifts), spatial extent (e.g. springs observed across 40 yards by 10 breadth), peculiarities (saltiest issue from middle of a rock), degree of saltness, observable effects downstream, and reasoning about source (distance to sea argument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine direct sensory observation (taste, visual extent), basic sampling/processing (boiling to obtain salt, note character of salt), and geographical reasoning about possible sources (distance to sea making marine origin improbable). Record how spring behaves under different river conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design criteria for river bridges to resist rapid/inundating streams
rubrics_metrics.description: Bridge failures ascribed to: (1) not being 'so multangular' as the robust bridge at St. Esprit, (2) lacking small arches dividing the feet of large ones (these parts suffer most), (3) pedestals not geometrically and exactly laid, lacking sufficient or gradually contracted projections so the stream's force is greater on the fabric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative analysis of surviving and failed bridges (Avignon vs Pont St. Esprit and Roman examples) to infer structural features that improve resistance: multi-angular planning, provision of small intermediate arches, and well-laid pedestals with contracted projections. Historical/empirical evidence from ruined and extant bridges informs recommended design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timber bridge construction specification (70-foot span without intermediate pillar)
rubrics_metrics.description: A timber bridge may be built 70 feet long without any pillar: consist of two timber arches with specified beam lengths (a c and b o = 28 ft; ab = 32 ft), large braces under angles, end walls with beams (bh and ad = 20 ft) and braces, optional oblique braces crossing the bridge, laid with planks and railed; length 70 ft; height 10 ft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives concrete component dimensions and placement (arches, braces, end walls, causeways) and suggests practical construction details for places where pillars cannot be built. This functions as a prescriptive specification rather than merely descriptive.
